3.text: cushion double bags of seal-skin, that were thrown across the sledge, and hung

4.text: from each side like saddle-bags. It is curious to note, that even now, when

5.text: another form of sledge has been universally adopted, the dog-driving people

6.text: on the Kolyma and Gishiga Rivers still use these saddle-bags for carrying

7.text: provisions, etc., though now a single bag would be more convenient. The

8.text: dog-teams were not so large as they are now. Krasheninnikoff says that the

9.text: average team was three pairs, while now it is twice as many. A two-pair

10.text: team was also much used. The driver frequently walked before the team,

11.text: especially in heavy snow, breaking the path with his snowshoes, and with voice

12.text: and motion urging the team to follow. This is still done in Kamchatka, and

13.text: the dogs follow obediently; while Kolyma dogs, should the driver go ahead

14.text: of them, would take it as a suggestion to stop. The method of walking

15.text: before the dogs, urging them to follow, is generally employed by Eskimo

16.text: drivers. It is interesting to note that two terms relating to dog-driving, and

17.text: used by the Russians in northeastern Siberia, — kayuˊr for the driver, and

18.text: oˊshtol for the brake, — are both of Kamchadal origin. In Kamchadal the

19.text: driver is called keˊyux; and the brake, oˊcxtlᴇnañ, from the verb t-ocxtaˊl-ɪck

20.text: (“I work with a brake”). This is the more curious, as the Cossacks went to

21.text: Kamchatka later than to the Kolyma and to Anadyr.

22.text: Among the Yukaghir of the Upper Kolyma, who are probably the most

23.text: primitive of all the tribes concerned, only a few dogs are attached to a sledge.

24.text: They are placed in tandem position, — not in pairs, but separately,¹ — three

25.text: or four dogs forming a team. There is no leader; but the men and women,

26.text: on snowshoes, walk on both sides of the team. By means of long straps

27.text: placed around the shoulders they help the dogs draw the sledge, and direct

28.text: their course. The same method of dog-driving was adopted by the Yukaghir

29.text: of the Lower Kolyma, of both the Anuis, and of the Omolon, as early as the

31.text: DOMESTICATION OF THE DOG. — The domestication of the dog in north-

32.text: eastern Asia surely preceded by a considerable period of time its adoption for

33.text: carrying-purposes. Lamut dogs, for instance, are now used exclusively for

34.text: hunting-pursuits. They scent squirrels and sables in the woods, overtake elk

35.text: and reindeer on the hard-crusted snow in the spring-time, and catch white and

36.text: red foxes on the open plain. Notwithstanding their fleetness, they are not

37.text: well fitted for driving, on account of their roaming disposition. On the other

38.text: hand, some European dogs, bought by Kamchatka drivers from merchant-ships,

39.text: prove to be well adapted for the harness, and are able to keep pace with the

40.text: native team, at least for short distances.
